title: Local DNS Attack Lab
description: Build a small authoritative/recursive BIND9 DNS environment, then attack it: hosts-file tampering, direct off-path response spoofing, and cache poisoning through the Answer, Authority, and Additional sections. Adapted from SEED Labs' Local DNS Attack Lab (Wenliang Du).

levels.title: Welcome: Local DNS Attack Lab
levels.content:
## Local DNS Attack Lab

DNS translates hostnames to IP addresses behind the scenes. Because most applications trust whatever answer comes back, an attacker who can inject a fake DNS response -- without ever touching the victim's machine -- can silently redirect users to a server of the attacker's choosing. This training walks through building a small, self-contained DNS environment and then attacking it, level by level: from a single compromised hosts file, up to poisoning an entire domain's worth of lookups in a recursive resolver's cache.

### Your three machines
- **user** -- an ordinary client machine, configured to use your own local DNS server.
- **dns** -- a BIND9 server you will configure, authoritative for `example.com`, and recursive for everything else.
- **attacker** -- your attack platform. It sits on the same local network as the other two and can observe their traffic.

### Rules
1. Attack only the machines inside this topology. All domain names used (`example.com`, `example.net`, `bank*.com`, `attacker32.com`, `google.com`) are fixed, reserved-for-documentation or lab-internal names -- nothing here ever leaves the sandbox network.
2. Work through the levels in order: each attack level builds on the DNS server you set up earlier.
3. Several levels have no visible 'did it work' signal from your own shell on purpose -- see the note below.

### A note on how this is graded
On a real network, nobody would tell an attacker whether their spoof landed -- they'd have to infer it from the DNS server's behavior changing downstream. The flags for Levels 5-8 work the same way: there is no sudo access on the `user` or `dns` machines (so nobody can simply hand-edit a zone file or `/etc/hosts` to fake a result), and each flag only appears in your home directory once an independent monitor has observed a genuinely spoofed packet arrive over the network from your attacker machine. Running the real attack is the only way to see the flag -- there is no shortcut, and that is intentional.

### Credits
Adapted from SEED Labs' *Local DNS Attack Lab* by Wenliang Du (Syracuse University), used here for non-commercial education under its original license. See ATTRIBUTION.txt for full credit and a list of deliberate deviations from the original lab.

levels.title: Access the Topology
levels.content:
## Accessing your machines

Open the topology view and access each machine's terminal (or SSH in directly once you have the sandbox's access info).

| Machine | Login user | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| user | `seed` | No sudo. Use the provided helper commands for any step that needs root (see each level). |
| dns | `seed` | No sudo. Same as above. |
| attacker | `seed` | Full sudo. This is your attack platform; Scapy and tcpdump are pre-installed. |

If a level says 'run `/usr/local/bin/dns-lab-...`', that program is a pre-built, narrowly-scoped helper -- it performs exactly one fixed administrative action and nothing else, which is why it doesn't need you to have general sudo rights.

levels.title: Task 1 -- Point the User Machine at Your DNS Server
levels.content:
## Task 1: Configure the User Machine

By default the `user` machine resolves names using whatever resolver the platform's DHCP hands it. We want it to ask *our* DNS server first instead. Normally this means editing `/etc/resolv.conf`, but DHCP clients overwrite that file on every lease renewal -- editing it directly doesn't stick.

The standard fix (and the one this lab uses) is to add the nameserver line to `/etc/resolvconf/resolv.conf.d/head` instead: its contents get prepended to the generated `/etc/resolv.conf` every time, so it survives DHCP renewals.

On `user`, run:
```
/usr/local/bin/dns-lab-set-resolver
```
This helper appends `nameserver 192.168.0.16` to the head file and re-runs `resolvconf -u` for you (it needs root; you don't have general sudo on this box, so the helper does exactly this one thing and nothing else).

Now confirm it worked:
```
dig www.example.com
```
**Answer with the exact value of the `SERVER:` line at the bottom of the `dig` output** (format `ip#port`) -- that's your evidence the response came from your own server, not some other resolver.
levels.solution: `dig` prints which server answered the query in its final statistics block, as `SERVER: <ip>#<port>(<ip>)`. After pointing resolv.conf.d/head at 192.168.0.16 and running `resolvconf -u`, every lookup (including `www.example.com`, which isn't resolvable yet since the zone doesn't exist until Task 3) should show `SERVER: 192.168.0.16#53` -- proof the query actually went to your DNS box rather than an upstream resolver.

hints.title: Which file actually sticks?
hints.content: DHCP rewrites /etc/resolv.conf directly on every renewal. resolvconf merges /etc/resolvconf/resolv.conf.d/head into the generated file instead of being overwritten by it.

hints.title: Where does dig show the server?
hints.content: Look at the last few lines of `dig`'s output, under ';; SERVER:'.

levels.title: Task 2 -- Stand Up the BIND9 Server
levels.content:
## Task 2: Set Up the Local DNS Server

`dns` already has BIND9 installed. For this lab we need two options set in `/etc/bind/named.conf.options`:

- a `dump-file` path, so you can inspect the resolver cache later, and
- DNSSEC validation turned off, since DNSSEC exists specifically to block the kind of spoofing this lab teaches, and we want to see the attacks work unobstructed.

On `dns`, run:
```
/usr/local/bin/dns-lab-configure-bind-options
```
This writes the options block and restarts `bind9` for you (again: no sudo on this box, so a single-purpose helper does it).

Inspect the file it wrote:
```
cat /etc/bind/named.conf.options
```
**What line in that file disables DNSSEC validation?** Answer with the exact directive (two words + its value).
levels.solution: `dnssec-enable no;` inside the options block. (The historical `dnssec-validation auto;` directive is commented out instead of being relied on, since in older BIND releases that alone doesn't fully disable validation.) You can confirm the dump-file is wired up with `sudo rndc dumpdb -cache` followed by inspecting `/var/cache/bind/dump.db` -- except you don't have sudo here either, which is deliberate; later levels show you the cache contents a different way.

levels.title: Task 3 -- Host an Authoritative Zone for example.com
levels.content:
## Task 3: Host a Zone on Your DNS Server

`example.com` is an IANA-reserved documentation domain, so it's safe to declare ourselves authoritative for it inside this sandbox. On `dns`, run:
```
/usr/local/bin/dns-lab-configure-zone
```
This adds a forward zone (`example.com`) and a matching reverse zone (`0.168.192.in-addr.arpa`) to `named.conf`, writes both zone files, and restarts `bind9`.

From `user` (which already points at this server from Task 1), run:
```
dig www.example.com +norecurse
```
You should see an `aa` flag in the response header -- your server answering as the *authority* for this domain, not as a recursive lookup.

**What IP address does `www.example.com` resolve to?**
levels.solution: 192.168.0.101, from the `www IN A 192.168.0.101` record in the zone file. The response carries the `aa` (Authoritative Answer) flag because the query falls inside a zone your own server is declared `type master` for -- it never has to ask anyone else.

hints.title: Where's the IP defined?
hints.content: It's an A record for the 'www' name inside the zone file the helper wrote.

levels.title: Task 4 -- Attack 1: Modify the Hosts File
levels.answer: ignored by dig, honored by ping and browsers
levels.content:
## Task 4: Modifying the Host File

`/etc/hosts` entries take priority over DNS lookups for most programs. Assume `user` is already compromised (you have a shell on it). Redirect `www.bank32.com` to any IP address you like (pick something obviously fake, e.g. `6.6.6.6`, so you can recognize it).

Run, on `user`:
```
/usr/local/bin/dns-lab-set-hosts-entry 6.6.6.6
```
(replace `6.6.6.6` with whatever IP you chose -- the helper validates it's a well-formed IPv4 address and writes exactly one line, `<ip> www.bank32.com`, into `/etc/hosts`).

Now compare:
```
dig www.bank32.com
ping -c1 www.bank32.com
```
**In one short phrase: which of `dig`/`ping` respects your hosts-file entry, and which ignores it?**
levels.solution: `dig` talks to a DNS server directly and never consults `/etc/hosts`, so it still fails (or returns whatever real-world answer exists for bank32.com) -- it shows your redirect had no effect on it. `ping`, like a web browser, goes through the system's standard name resolution (`getaddrinfo`/NSS), which checks `/etc/hosts` before ever asking a DNS server -- so it picks up your fake IP immediately. This is exactly why hosts-file tampering is invisible to DNS-level monitoring: it never touches the network at all.

hints.title: Two different resolution paths
hints.content: dig is a pure DNS client. ping uses the OS's normal name resolution (NSS), which checks /etc/hosts first.

levels.title: Task 5 -- Attack 2: Directly Spoof a Response to the User
levels.content:
## Task 5: Directly Spoofing a Response to the User

`user` has NOT been compromised this time. You (on `attacker`) are just another host on the same LAN. If you can see the DNS query `user` sends out, you can race the real DNS server to reply first with a forged answer -- and if your forged packet satisfies every field the real reply would (source IP/port, destination IP/port, transaction ID, question section), `user` has no way to tell the difference.

From `user`, trigger a fresh query (the zone for `example.net` doesn't exist anywhere in this sandbox, so without your interference the query will simply time out):
```
dig www.example.net
```
On `attacker`, write a Scapy script that:
1. Sniffs for `user`'s outgoing query for `www.example.net` (filter on `udp and dst port 53`),
2. Builds a spoofed reply with the DNS server's IP as source, `user`'s IP and source port as destination, the same transaction ID and question section, and an Answer section mapping `www.example.net` to an IP of your choice, and
3. Sends it back to `user` before the (nonexistent) real answer ever could.

The lab guide's `4 Guideline` section has a worked Scapy example you can adapt (it spoofs a different query name, but the structure is identical).

Re-run `dig www.example.net` from `user` while your script is sniffing/spoofing and confirm you get your forged IP back.

**Once a real spoofed packet from your attacker machine has been observed landing on `user`, your flag will appear at `~/flag_task5.txt` on the `user` machine. Submit its contents.**

Nothing you do on `dns` or `user` themselves can produce this flag -- it only appears once your forged packet has actually crossed the network, which is the whole point of the exercise.
levels.solution: A background watcher on `user` (not reachable or editable by the student -- there is no sudo on this box) passively inspects incoming UDP/53 traffic. It only reveals the flag once it sees a DNS response (`qr=1`) whose answer section names `www.example.net`, arriving from the attacker machine's real IP address. A correct solution script: sniffs `udp and dst port 53` on attacker's interface; on each packet, checks `pkt[DNS].qd.qname` for `www.example.net`; builds the reply with swapped src/dst IP and port, the DNS server's IP as the spoofed source, the same `id`, `qr=1`, `aa=1`, `rd=0`, one Answer RR, and sends it with `send()`. See instructor-solutions/scripts/attack_task5_spoof.py for a tested reference implementation (instructors only -- not shipped to students).

hints.title: Which fields must match exactly?
hints.content: Source IP = real DNS server's IP. Destination IP/port = the exact IP and source port the query came from. Transaction ID = pkt[DNS].id. Question section = pkt[DNS].qd, unchanged.

hints.title: Timing
hints.content: Since example.net isn't hosted anywhere in this sandbox, there's no real reply racing you -- you just need your script actively sniffing before you run dig.

hints.title: Still not seeing the flag?
hints.content: Check your script is sending from the attacker machine's OWN real interface/IP (you're only spoofing the DNS header's claimed source IP, not the Ethernet/IP packet's actual origin) -- the grading watcher specifically looks for packets that physically arrived from your attacker box.

levels.title: Task 6 -- Attack 3: DNS Cache Poisoning
levels.content:
## Task 6: DNS Cache Poisoning

Spoofing the user directly only lasts for one query. A much more durable attack targets `dns` itself: if you can spoof the response it receives when IT asks upstream for `www.example.net`, the forged answer gets cached and served to every future querent -- including users you never directly interacted with.

From `attacker`, write a Scapy script that sniffs for `dns`'s outgoing query for `www.example.net` and races a spoofed answer back to `dns`'s resolver port before any real upstream reply could arrive. Trigger the query from `user`:
```
dig www.example.net
```
Give your spoofed record a long TTL so it sticks.

**Once a genuine spoofed packet from `attacker` is observed arriving at `dns` and the forged `www.example.net` record has been cached, your flag appears at `~/flag_task6.txt` on the `dns` machine.**
levels.solution: Same technique as Task 5, but targeting `dns`'s own query socket instead of `user`'s: sniff on attacker's interface for `dns`'s outbound query, spoof a reply with a plausible upstream IP as source, `dns`'s IP/port as destination, the correct transaction ID, an Answer RR for `www.example.net`, and a large `ttl` (e.g. 259200) so it persists in cache. See instructor-solutions/scripts/attack_task6_cache_poison.py.

hints.title: What changed from Task 5?
hints.content: You're now racing the query that the DNS SERVER sends out, not the one from the user -- sniff/spoof against dns's egress, not user's.

hints.title: Make it stick
hints.content: Set a large TTL in your DNSRR so the poisoned entry survives in the cache rather than expiring immediately.

levels.title: Task 7 -- Attack 4: Poisoning via the Authority Section
levels.content:
## Task 7: DNS Cache Poisoning -- Targeting the Authority Section

Task 6's attack only poisons one hostname at a time. A single spoofed reply can do far more damage if, alongside the Answer section, it also forges an **Authority section** NS record claiming that `attacker32.com` is now the nameserver for the *entire* `example.net` domain. If `dns` caches that claim, every future `*.example.net` lookup gets redirected to a server you control -- no further spoofing required.

From `attacker`, extend your Task 6 script: in addition to the Answer section, add an Authority-section `DNSRR` of type `NS` for `example.net` pointing at `attacker32.com`. Trigger a fresh query from `user` (`dig www.example.net`, after flushing is not available to you -- just pick a name you haven't already poisoned, or wait and re-run).

**Once `dns` has genuinely cached an Authority-section NS record for `example.net` pointing at `attacker32.com`, delivered by a real packet from `attacker`, your flag appears at `~/flag_task7.txt` on the `dns` machine.**
levels.solution: Add a second `DNSRR(rrname='example.net', type='NS', ttl=259200, rdata='attacker32.com')` to the `ns=` argument of the spoofed `DNS()` packet, and set `nscount=1` to match. BIND accepts in-bailiwick Authority-section glue from a response it already trusts, which is exactly why this attack works at all. See instructor-solutions/scripts/attack_task7_authority_spoof.py.

hints.title: DNS section, not Answer
hints.content: Use the ns= field of the Scapy DNS() constructor, not an=. Set nscount to match how many records you put there.

hints.title: rrname for the NS record
hints.content: The NS record's rrname is the domain being delegated (example.net), and its rdata is the nameserver you're claiming authority as (attacker32.com).

levels.title: Task 8 -- Attack 5: Extending Impact to Another Domain
levels.content:
## Task 8: Targeting Another Domain

Task 7 hijacked `example.net`. Since a spoofed reply's Authority section can carry more than one NS record, you can piggyback a second, completely unrelated domain onto the same forged packet. Add a second Authority-section NS record claiming `attacker32.com` is also now authoritative for `google.com` -- even though the query that triggered your spoofed reply was for `www.example.net`, not anything under `google.com`.

From `attacker`, extend your script once more: keep the Task 7 Answer + Authority(example.net) records, and add a THIRD record to the Authority section: `DNSRR(rrname='google.com', type='NS', ttl=259200, rdata='attacker32.com')`. Update `nscount` accordingly. Trigger with a fresh `dig www.example.net` from `user`.

**Once `dns` has cached an Authority-section NS record for `google.com` pointing at `attacker32.com`, delivered by a real packet from `attacker`, your flag appears at `~/flag_task8.txt` on the `dns` machine.**
levels.solution: `ns=NSsec1/NSsec2` in Scapy, where NSsec1 is the example.net record from Task 7 and NSsec2 is `DNSRR(rrname='google.com', type='NS', ttl=259200, rdata='attacker32.com')`, with `nscount=2`. This demonstrates that a single successful spoof against one domain's lookup can be abused to poison records for domains that were never even queried -- as long as the resolver doesn't reject out-of-bailiwick glue. See instructor-solutions/scripts/attack_task8_authority_multi_spoof.py.

hints.title: Two NS records, not two packets
hints.content: Both Authority-section NS records go in the SAME spoofed reply -- chain them with Scapy's / operator in the ns= field.

hints.title: nscount
hints.content: Don't forget to bump nscount to 2 to match the two chained NS records, or BIND may not parse the section the way you expect.

levels.title: Task 9 -- Attack 6: Poisoning the Additional Section
levels.content:
## Task 9: Targeting the Additional Section

The Additional section of a DNS reply usually supplies IP addresses ('glue') for hostnames mentioned in the Authority section, saving the resolver an extra round trip. Extend your spoofed reply from Task 7/8 with an Additional section containing three A records:

1. `attacker32.com -> 1.2.3.4` (glue for your own forged NS record),
2. `ns.example.net -> 5.6.7.8` (glue for a name mentioned in the Authority section),
3. `www.facebook.com -> 3.4.5.6` (an entirely unrelated name, 'helpfully' thrown in).

Send this reply and inspect what actually ends up cached. You don't need a new attacker script for this -- reason about it from what you've already learned about how resolvers decide what glue to trust.

**In one word: what is the general name for the rule a well-behaved resolver uses to decide which Additional-section records it's allowed to cache (hint: it only trusts glue that falls 'in-domain' relative to what the reply is actually authoritative for)?**
levels.solution: **Bailiwick** checking. A resolver following bailiwick rules only accepts/caches additional-section glue for names that fall within the zone the response is actually authoritative for. Records 1 and 2 are in-bailiwick (they glue names that were themselves just introduced in the Authority/Answer sections of the SAME reply, within domains this reply is speaking for) and get cached. Record 3, `www.facebook.com`, is completely unrelated to anything this reply is authoritative over -- a bailiwick-aware resolver discards it rather than letting any attacker who can answer one query silently rewrite unrelated domains.

hints.title: Think about scope, not content
hints.content: It's not about whether a record LOOKS plausible -- it's about whether the name belongs to a zone this particular reply has any business speaking for.

hints.title: One more hint
hints.content: The term also appears in RFC discussions of cache poisoning defenses; it describes which 'turf' a DNS answer is allowed to make claims about.
